plants.scientific_name: Gymnocalycium mihanovichii (red scion) on a green rootstock
plants.location: Porch shelf, between the crown of thorns, boobie cactus and haworthia
plants.container: Black nursery pot, gritty mix
plants.id_basis: A bright red, ribbed globe with white-tufted spines sitting on a green stem is a grafted red Gymnocalycium mihanovichii. The red colour has no chlorophyll, so it only lives because it is grafted onto the green rootstock.
plants.id_alternatives:
Gymnocalycium mihanovichii 'Hibotan' / 'Ruby Ball'
Other coloured Gymnocalycium grafts (yellow, orange, pink)
plants.id_improve:
Side view of the graft union to see which rootstock it is on
Tag or seller name if you want the colour-form name
plants.temp_notes: Tender: the rootstock chills and rots below about 45 F and freezes at 32 F. Cold plus wet soil is the usual killer.
plants.humidity_notes: Likes dry air. Wet, cold soil rots the graft.
plants.light_notes: The red top scorches in hard afternoon sun and fades in deep shade. The green rootstock keeps growing and can shade out the red top.
plants.winter_summary: Tender grafted cactus. Bring it inside before nights fall under 50 F and keep it dry and bright.
plants.winter_triggers: Target Nov 1; required before any night under 45 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Nov 1, before the first night forecast under 50 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
From November water only about once a month, just enough that the mix never turns to dust.
Never stand the pot in a saucer of water.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Keep it above 50 F, ideally 55-65 F on a cool bright windowsill, away from heater vents.
Cut off any shoots growing from the green rootstock; they will overgrow the red top.
plants.health_summary: Deep red, firm and plump with a healthy orange offset next to it. No rot, soft spots or pests visible.
plants.health_observations:
Intense red colour with no browning
A small orange offset (pup) sits on the soil
Dried leaf debris on the soil surface
Rootstock is dark green and firm
plants.health_steps:
Remove the dead leaf debris from the soil surface
Keep the soil nearly dry through winter
Leave the pup until it is marble-sized, then twist it off and root it in gritty mix if you want a second plant

plants.scientific_name: Agave sp. (possibly A. parryi, A. ovatifolia or A. americana type)
plants.location: Porch shelf / front table
plants.container: Clear plastic tub with a bark and gravel mix
plants.id_basis: Thick, rigid blue-gray leaves in a tight rosette with small teeth along the edges and bud-print impressions on the leaf surface are typical of Agave. The species cannot be told from this angle.
plants.id_alternatives:
Agave parryi
Agave ovatifolia (whale's tongue)
Agave americana
Aloe or Manfreda (less likely: bud prints point to Agave)
plants.id_improve:
Side view of the whole rosette
Close-up of a leaf edge (tooth size and colour) and the sharp tip
Tag, receipt or where it came from
plants.temp_notes: Agaves of this type usually take 15-25 F when dry. In a pot the roots are exposed, and cold plus wet leaves rots the rosette. In a wet El Nino winter, keeping it dry matters more than the exact temperature.
plants.humidity_notes: Thrives in dry air. Stagnant, humid cold is what harms it.
plants.light_notes: Bright sun keeps the blue colour and tight shape. It stretches and weakens indoors.
plants.winter_summary: Probably hardy to about 20 F but a potted agave in a cold, wet winter can rot. Keep it dry and covered on freeze nights.
plants.winter_triggers: Cover at 28 F; move under the porch roof for any wet freeze.
plants.winter_steps:
Move it under the porch roof so winter rain does not collect in the crown.
Cover with frost cloth at 28 F or below (never plastic touching the leaves) and remove the cover above 35 F.
No watering from November to February unless the mix has been bone dry for weeks and it is above 50 F.
Raise the pot on feet so it never sits in water.
plants.indoor_setup:
If a hard freeze below 20 F is forecast, move it into the garage or a covered corner for the night. It needs light, not warmth.
Handle with gloves and eye protection: the tip is sharp.
plants.health_summary: Firm, upright blue-gray leaves with no soft or mushy areas. A few small reddish-brown specks near the leaf bases and slight tip browning.

Surface of the mix is dry
plants.health_steps:
Check leaf bases and the crown with a flashlight for scale or mealybugs
Dab a speck with rubbing alcohol on a swab to see if it is an insect
Keep water out of the crown

plants.location: Porch shelf / front table
plants.container: Terracotta pot with a pumice and bark mix
plants.id_basis: Woody, branching stems topped with flat rosettes of spoon-shaped burgundy leaves with a green centre and fine hairs on the margins. The genus is certain; the cultivar is a best guess.
plants.id_alternatives:
Aeonium arboreum 'Zwartkop'
Aeonium 'Garnet'
Aeonium 'Velour'
Other dark Aeonium hybrids

Photo of the whole plant from the side

plants.temp_notes: Aeoniums grow in cool weather and rest in summer heat. Frost burns the leaves below about 30 F and stems rot after hard freezes.
plants.humidity_notes: Tolerates humid winters if the mix drains.
plants.light_notes: Dark colour comes from sun and leaves turn green in shade. Hot afternoon sun burns them.
plants.winter_summary: Winter is its growing season, so it tolerates cool weather but not hard freezes. Protect below 30 F.
plants.winter_triggers: Cover at 30 F; garage or porch at 26 F or in a wet freeze.
plants.winter_steps:
Cover at 30 F or below (frost cloth/sheet draped to the ground over a frame; frost cloth buys roughly 6-8 F). Bring in or move into the garage at 26 F or in a multi-day freeze.
Water the day before a freeze (moist soil holds heat) but keep the plant dry the rest of winter; skip watering when it is below 40 F.
Cluster pots against a south/east wall under the roof, away from north wind, and pile mulch or leaves around the pots.
Stop nitrogen fertilizer now; new tender growth freezes first.
Water lightly through the cool growing season only if the mix is dry and it is above 45 F; never leave it sitting wet in the cold.
plants.indoor_setup: A garage with a window or an unheated sunroom works well: it needs light and temperatures above 28 F.

plants.id_basis: A rosette of long floating stalks with rounded blades and swollen, bulbous stalk bases in a bucket of water matches water hyacinth. The stalks are long and thin and the feathery roots are not visible in the photo.
plants.id_alternatives:

Another floating or marginal aquatic plant

plants.temp_notes: Growth stops below about 55 F, leaves blacken at a light frost and a hard freeze kills it. Water in a bucket buffers the cold slightly.

Read the TPWD rule in the notes first.
Whatever you decide, never pour the water or plants into a drain, ditch, creek or pond. Bag and bin the plants, or let them dry out completely.

Shallow warm water in a clear tub under a grow light.
Add a very small amount of liquid fertilizer.
Expect it to struggle indoors; it is a sun-loving summer plant.

Long thin stalks (stretched in low light)

plants.notes: Texas Parks and Wildlife lists water hyacinth among harmful or potentially harmful exotic aquatic plants. Its rules make it unlawful to possess or transport listed plants without a permit and do not mention an exception for home or ornamental containers. Check with TPWD before keeping it. plants.light_notes: Hot Texas afternoon sun scorches the leaves. Deep shade cuts flowering.
plants.winter_summary: Moderately hardy evergreen shrub. Protect it from hard freezes, especially in a pot.
plants.winter_triggers: Cover at 30 F; porch or garage at 25 F or below.
plants.winter_steps:
Cover at 30 F or below (frost cloth/sheet draped to the ground over a frame; frost cloth buys roughly 6-8 F). Bring in or move into the garage at 25 F or in a multi-day freeze.
Water the day before a freeze (moist soil holds heat) but keep the plant dry the rest of winter; skip watering when it is below 40 F.
Cluster pots against a south/east wall under the roof, away from north wind, and pile mulch or leaves around the pots.
Stop nitrogen fertilizer now; new tender growth freezes first.
Mulch the surface of the pot with 2-3 in of pine bark.
Do not prune in winter; wait until after the last frost.
plants.indoor_setup: If brought in: bright window, 60-70 F and about 50% humidity. Gardenias drop buds in dry air.
plants.health_summary: Many leaves have brown scorched margins and the newest leaves are yellow-green with darker veins, which looks like iron chlorosis. Growth is dense and active.
plants.health_observations:
Brown crisp leaf edges and tips on many leaves
Pale new leaves with green veins (typical iron deficiency)
Round Rock's alkaline water and soil raise the pH
Pot has an inner and outer pot: check that water is not pooling
No visible pests or buds
plants.health_steps:
Test the pH of the mix and water (target 5.0-6.0)
In spring apply chelated iron or an acid-loving fertilizer (azalea or camellia type)
Water with rainwater or let tap water stand
Check leaf undersides for scale, whitefly and sooty mould
Give it morning sun and afternoon shade, and mulch with pine bark
No fertilizer in cold weather

plants.winter_summary: Tropical tree. Bring it in before nights fall under 55 F.
plants.winter_triggers: Target Nov 1; before any night under 50 F.
plants.winter_steps:
Target: indoors by about Nov 1, before the first night forecast under 50 F.
Pre-move: rinse the leaves with a hose, check undersides and stem nodes for spider mites, mealybugs, scale and fungus gnats, treat with insecticidal soap or neem, then quarantine 2 weeks away from other houseplants.
Acclimate in two steps to limit leaf drop: about a week on the covered porch or in the garage, then inside.
Do not repot or fertilize for the move; trim only dead tissue.
Wear gloves: the sap irritates the skin.
plants.indoor_setup:
Indoors: within 3 ft of an east or south window, or under a full-spectrum grow light 12-14 h/day at 6-12 in. Winter sun in Round Rock is only ~4.5-6 hours of real sunshine per day in Dec-Jan, so supplement.
Indoor winter air is typically 20-35% RH; raise it with a humidifier (target 50-60%), grouping plants, or a pebble tray, and keep plants away from heater vents.
Water when the top 2 in dry; reduce in winter.
Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth once a month.
